title: Methods
text:
This analysis fits a marked Log Gaussian Cox Process (LGCP) to aggravated assault point patterns in Minneapolis, 2020–2022, using the NIMBLE probabilistic programming framework.


Let s_i denote the location of event i. The intensity \lambda(s) follows:
\log \lambda(s,t) = \mathbf{x}(s)^\top \boldsymbol{\beta} + \log \rho(s) + W(s) + \delta_{1,t}
where \mathbf{x}(s) are fixed-effect covariates (intercept, distance to water), \rho(s) is a population density offset, W(s) is a zero-mean Gaussian process spatial random effect, and \delta_{1,t} is a year random effect.



Each event carries a binary mark Y_i \in \{0,1\} (domestic / non-domestic). Given the event location:
\text{logit}\,P(Y_i = 1 \mid s_i) = \mathbf{z}(s_i)^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma} + \delta_{2,t}
where \mathbf{z}(s_i) includes intercept, distance to water, and a smoothed domestic-call-type flag.



The GP uses a low-rank approximation with n_K adaptive knots (denser in high-crime areas) and exponential covariance C(d) = \sigma^2 \exp(-\phi \, d). The range parameter \phi is estimated via empirical variogram on the raw point pattern. The non-centered parameterization W^\star = L\mathbf{z},\; \mathbf{z} \sim N(0,I) (where L is the Cholesky factor of the knot covariance) improves MCMC mixing.




Chains: 3 parallel chains via R parallel
Iterations: 150,000 total; 75,000 burn-in; thinning = 10
Posterior samples: 7,500 per chain
Convergence: Gelman-Rubin \hat{R} on \boldsymbol{\beta}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}, year REs, variance components

title: Understanding Domestic Violence
text:
What Is Domestic Violence?
Domestic violence is a pattern of behavior used by one partner to maintain power and control over another in an intimate relationship. It encompasses physical, emotional, psychological, sexual, and financial abuse.
Contrary to common perception, domestic violence is not confined to low-income communities or any single demographic. It affects people across all income levels, ethnicities, ages, and genders.

title: Understanding Domestic Violence
text:
Warning Signs
In a partner’s behavior: - Extreme jealousy or possessiveness - Controlling finances, movements, or social relationships - Humiliation, belittling, or public embarrassment - Threats of harm to you, children, or pets - Minimizing or denying abusive behavior
Physical indicators: - Unexplained bruises or injuries - Injuries inconsistent with offered explanations - A partner who insists on accompanying to medical appointments

title: Understanding Domestic Violence
text:
Cycle of Violence
Research documents a recurring pattern in many abusive relationships:

Tension building — stress accumulates, survivor “walks on eggshells”
Incident — explosion of abusive behavior
Reconciliation — apologies, promises to change, honeymoon period
Calm — incident minimized or forgotten

This cycle can repeat many times and typically escalates in severity over time.

title: Understanding Domestic Violence
text:
Why Study DV Spatially?
Spatial analysis of domestic assault calls can help: - Allocate resources — identify neighborhoods where intervention programs have highest marginal impact - Evaluate policy — measure whether interventions shift the intensity surface over time - Understand context — examine how population density, infrastructure, and socioeconomic factors correlate with assault risk
This site presents one such analysis for Minneapolis, 2020–2022, using a Bayesian marked Log Gaussian Cox Process.

The statistics on this site represent reported aggravated assault records. Domestic violence is systemically underreported; true prevalence is substantially higher.
